item.title: 1,500-unit ice-water program ships to UK distributor
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
The last container of the program left our Dayawan facility this week: 1,500 ice-water units built on the F900 platform, bound for a UK home-appliance distributor serving retail chains. The line started as a spec conversation and ended as a fully certified retail SKU — here is how the weeks were spent.

The brief came straight from the case file: a differentiated ice-water line for European retail, food-contact compliance on the water path, and a launch window that left no room for re-work. Volume was set at 1,500 units for the first run, and the program was planned backwards from the shelf date.

How the program ran

It followed the standard OEM route. A requirement talk fixed market, volume and certification scope; concept development translated that into appearance renders and a technical proposal; then a frozen spec sheet became the single reference for sampling, production and inspection — so when the four-week clock started, nothing on the critical path was still moving. Every checkpoint on that route had a named owner on both sides, which is the unglamorous reason the window held.

Configuring the F900 platform

The F900 platform provided the base: ice-cold dispensing at 5–8 °C, an RO + UV dual-purification stage in the water path, and dual-algorithm control holding output steady through back-to-back pours. On top of that, housing and packaging were customized to the distributor's retail brand — finish, branding and carton layout locked together with the technical spec, so production and shelf presentation moved as one program.

Certification and pre-shipment inspection

CE marking and food-contact documentation were handled inside the four-week window, alongside pre-shipment inspection of the finished units. Nothing in that window was compressed by skipping steps — it was compressed by deciding things early: food-contact compliance was specified at the material level at the start, not tested into the product at the end. The documentation package shipped with the container, so the distributor's compliance team had every file on record before the goods arrived.

What is in the container

For teams scoping a similar program, the short version of what shipped:

  • 1,500 ice-water units on the F900 platform
  • Housing and packaging customized to the retail brand
  • CE marking and food-contact documentation for the water path
  • Pre-shipment inspection records for the full batch

The sample quality and certification support won the shelf slot, and a reorder is already in discussion. Programs of this shape — proven platform, brand-specific housing, tight certification window — are the core of what we do. If one is on your roadmap for next season, the structure is the same: one conversation, one spec sheet, one window.

item.title: Three seconds to 95 °C: how thick-film heating works
item.dc:creator: dazhen-rd
item.content:encoded:
Most water dispensers still heat a tank and wait. Ours prints the heater onto the water path and switches it on demand — here is what that difference means in practice, and why OEM buyers keep asking about it.

A printed element, not a coiled wire

The core is a nano rare-earth thick-film element: a heating circuit printed directly onto the water path, rather than a coiled metal wire wrapped around a tank. Power goes in, the film heats the flowing water, and dispensing temperature arrives in about three seconds — the platform our R&D center first stood up in 2014, and the one every 18E faucet and F900 station still builds on today.

What it means for a program

Speed is the headline; stability is the reason programs stay on the platform. A dual-algorithm control module watches the element and the flow, holding the set temperature within one degree — cup after cup, season after season.

Most buyers are surprised there is no wire to scale and no tank to pre-heat — the heating surface is the water path itself.

— Dazhen R&D team

The practical points, as an OEM buyer would put them:

  • Three seconds from ambient to 95 °C at the spout
  • Temperature held within one degree by dual-algorithm control
  • No stored tank — no re-boiling, no standing hot water
  • Compact formats: faucet, built-in and under-sink platforms

Where it ships today

The platform ships today across the 18E instant-heat faucet line and the F900-QC built-in drinking station — the same element behind different housings, displays and duty cycles. If your market needs proof before volume, samples ship with lab reports covering heating curves, flow rates and safety tests.

item.title: Bangkok recap: what Southeast Asian buyers asked us
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
We spent the show week in Bangkok meeting distributors, retail groups and hotel engineering teams from across Southeast Asia. Between the samples on the booth table and the spec sheets that left with visitors, five questions came up again and again — here is the short version, with the answers we gave on the spot.

A note on who asked what: distributors leaned toward certification and MOQ questions, hotel engineering teams toward retrofit and maintenance, retail groups toward sparkling SKUs. The overlap was the interesting part — by the last day, most conversations touched all three.

1. What certifications can you support?

Production runs on an ISO 9001 certified line and the factory is BSCI-audited. Every water path is built to food-contact material standards, and applicable models carry CE and CB marking. Buyers planning retail chains also asked about paperwork: the certification package we shipped with the UK ice-water program — CE files, food-contact documentation, inspection records — is the reference for what arrives with the container.

For education and medical deployments, the questions shift to safe-temperature dispensing and child-proof controls; those requirements slot into the same spec process rather than a separate track.

2. Will sparkling water hold its fizz in this heat?

It was a fair question at booth temperature. Our sparkling-faucet platform was tuned for tropical ambient temperatures during the 1,800-unit Thailand retail program: carbonation levels were adjusted so the pour stays consistent in a warm kitchen, not just in a temperate test lab. That program is now in production for a family-oriented retail lineup.

Visitors poured for themselves at the demo unit — the difference between a temperate-climate carbonation spec and a tuned one is visible in the glass. For programs shipping to warm markets we validate carbonation at high ambient temperatures as part of the spec, which is exactly what the Thailand program signed off.

3. What is the minimum order — really?

One hundred units. That is the MOQ we quote for an OEM program, with a typical lead time of four to six weeks from frozen spec to container loading. Visitors were planning everything from a single retail SKU to a full housewares line, so we walked through how volume changes tooling and packaging decisions — not the entry ticket.

For the record, the MOQ covers a customization on an existing platform — housing color and finish, spout geometry, display language, packaging. Ground-up product development is a different conversation with a different calendar.

4. Do you make hot and cold in one unit?

Yes, and it was one of the most-tested demos on the table. Dazhen launched the industry's first instant hot-and-cold integrated unit in 2021, and the current F900 platform serves three-second hot water and 5–8 °C ice water from one under-sink station, with RO and UV purification in the water path.

The dual-algorithm control module is what makes the pairing work: it watches the element and the flow, holding set temperatures within one degree. In a hotel retrofit that means hundreds of rooms pouring the same cup — installed floor by floor, around event schedules.

5. How do we start?

The way every program in this blog started: a conversation about your market, expected volume and certification scope. We recommend a platform, you review the concept and cost breakdown, and the frozen spec sheet becomes the single reference for sampling and production. Samples ship with lab reports — heating curves, flow rates, safety and endurance tests — so your team can validate in-market before committing to volume.

The show's own lesson for us: the questions are converging. Certification scope, tropical performance and integration used to be three separate conversations — in Bangkok they arrived as one brief. If yours was not on this list, send it over — an engineer replies within one business day. Bring the volume you have in mind; the timeline comes back with it.

item.title: 1,800 sparkling-water units enter production for Thailand

item.content:encoded:
Spec confirmed, line running, first articles approved: production is underway on 1,800 sparkling-water units for a Thailand retail program. The order moved from sampling to volume this month on the sparkling-faucet platform, tuned for a tropical market. Production follows the sampling round that settled carbonation, finish and packaging in one pass.

The brief came straight from the case file: a sparkling-water appliance tuned to tropical climates and family usage, for a Southeast-Asian retail group. Family retail in warm markets is exactly the segment the sparkling-faucet platform was tuned for.

Why carbonation needed tuning

Southeast-Asian retail buyers do not test appliances in a temperate lab — they plug them into a warm kitchen. For this program, carbonation levels were adjusted for tropical ambient temperatures so the pour stays consistent from the first glass of a hot afternoon to the last. The client raised it at the requirement stage, and it shaped the spec sheet from day one. Consistency, not peak fizz, is what families notice: the second glass has to pour like the first.

Packaging for family retail

The program is aimed at family households, so the unboxing had to work without a translator. Units ship with a bilingual quick-start guide covering installation, first use and daily care, and the retail carton layout was confirmed alongside the technical spec rather than after it — one package moving at the speed of the program. The guide ships in the box, not as a download; family retail lives or dies by the first ten minutes after opening.

What happens next

First articles were approved against the frozen spec sheet — the same document the client signed at the start, which keeps the definition of good stable from sample to container. The run continues through in-line inspection and batch traceability on the ISO 9001 line, then into export cartons with a documented container loading plan, with certification documentation shipping alongside the goods. Inspection records follow each batch, so the retail group can trace any unit back through the line. The retail launch calendar drives the schedule from here — the production window was planned around it from the start.

From sample to shelf

The program followed the standard route every Dazhen OEM program takes: requirement talk, concept development, a frozen spec sheet, sampling with lab reports, then production. For sparkling SKUs the interesting engineering is in the tuning — carbonation behavior, temperature performance, packaging language — because the platform itself is proven volume. That is the quiet advantage of building on a platform that already ships: the questions left to answer are market questions, not feasibility questions.

We will follow up once the first containers land and sell-through data starts coming back from the retail partner.

item.title: From spec to container: an OEM program diary
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Marketing timelines make OEM programs look like a straight line. In practice, the weeks bend around approvals, testing slots and shipping calendars — so when a recent custom program moved from frozen spec to container loading, we kept notes. Here is the diary, week by week, with notes on where the time actually went. Total elapsed time from first call to container: inside the four-to-six-week band we quote for programs of this scope.

A note on scope: this was a mid-volume customization on an existing platform — housing color and finish, spout geometry, display language and packaging — not a ground-up development. Ground-up programs add concept iterations on top of this skeleton.

The habit started as an internal one: program managers wanted a record of where estimates diverged from reality, so the next quote could be honest instead of optimistic. This entry keeps numbers and names general — the shape of the weeks is the point.

Week 0 — The requirement talk

The program opened with a focused conversation: target market, expected volume, price band and the certifications that had to be on file. From that brief we recommended the platform and drafted the project timeline. Three deliverables left the week: the requirement brief, a platform shortlist and the project timeline. A handful of emails and one call — the cheapest days of the whole program, and the ones that decided everything downstream.

Weeks 1–2 — Concept development

Our industrial designers translated the brief into appearance concepts and a complete technical proposal. The client reviewed renders, functions and costs before any tooling was committed — which is the entire point of the phase: changes here cost a slide deck, changes later cost a production line. The phase closed with three documents on the client's desk: concept renders, a technical proposal and a cost breakdown.

Week 2 — Spec confirmation

One week, one document. Every parameter was locked — heating power, dispensing modes, materials, surface finish, packaging layout — and the frozen spec sheet became the single reference for everything that followed. When a question came up during the run, the answer was already on file; that is what "frozen" is for. Deliverables: the spec sheet, the material list and the packaging die-line.

Weeks 3–4 — Sampling and testing

Prototype units were built and run through lab testing: heating curves, flow rates, safety and endurance. Samples shipped with the reports so the client's team could validate them in-market — their climate, their water, their outlets. Approval came back with two small packaging notes, folded into the run before the line started. Deliverables: the prototype, the lab report and the test data.

Weeks 4–5 — Production and QC

The run went onto the ISO 9001 certified line with in-line inspection at key stations and batch traceability from component intake to final assembly. This is the uneventful part, and that is deliberate: nothing dramatic happened in weeks four and five because the dramatic options had been designed out in weeks one through four. Deliverables: the QC report, inspection records and production photos.

For context on scale: the program sits above our 100-unit MOQ tier, on the customization route where the platform is proven and the variables are cosmetic and regional. The same production discipline applies whether the batch is a hundred units or a thousand — in-line inspection does not care.

Weeks 5–6 — Packaging and shipping

Units moved into retail-ready export cartons, the container loading plan was documented with photos, and export documents were handled by our team. The container left Dayawan on schedule. Deliverables: the loading plan, container photos and export documents.

Ongoing — After delivery

The one-year program warranty is now running, with spare parts and updates available throughout the cycle. Field feedback feeds into the next batch iteration — the diary does not really end at the container; it changes hands.

The diary's honest addendum: the unlisted days matter too. Holidays, the client's own audit season and one shipping slot that moved twice all bent the calendar — none of them broke it, because the timeline carried buffer written in at week zero. Plan the buffer before you need it; that is the whole trick.

Where the time really goes

Read back, the notes say one thing: the calendar holds because the front of the program holds. The spec sheet and the sample report are the two documents that save the most time later — which is why real hours go into both before the line starts. The four-to-six-week lead time we quote is not a promise to hurry; it is a promise that nothing after week two is discovering anything new.

One more observation from the notes: the client's own approval chain was on the critical path more often than our production was. That is normal, and it is manageable — as long as approval dates are written into the timeline at week zero, not discovered at week four.

If you are planning a program, expect the same shape. The weeks will bend — around an approval, a holiday, a shipping slot — but on a proven platform they bend predictably.

item.title: UAE hotel program: 220 rooms move into production
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Venue-wide drinking stations for a Middle East hotel group — 220 rooms — have moved from sampling to production. The program covers room and corridor units across a renovating events property, and it has been a textbook exercise in engineering-scale delivery: consistent performance across hundreds of rooms, on a renovation calendar, in a building that never closes.

Hotel programs sit in our Hotel & Engineering line for a reason: they compress every OEM discipline — finish matching, duty cycles, phased rollout, central maintenance — into one specification. This one is worth a public recap because it cleared each hurdle cleanly.

Production follows the approved samples; the sampling round settled finish, fit and reporting in one pass, which is why the program could hold its renovation-calendar dates. Engineering-scale delivery is mostly about not improvising: the same unit behavior, the same finish, the same reporting, room after room.

What the property needed

The renovation's interior package set the tone for everything. Wall-mounted and built-in units were specified with brushed finishes to match it, and the specification sheets were written against the interior language, not adapted to it afterwards. When the drinking station has to read as part of the room — not as equipment in it — finish decisions are engineering decisions.

Why the mock-up room mattered

Before any production commitment, we built a mock-up room. The client's engineering and design teams approved finish, placement and dispensing behavior in a single session — the mock-up room process made approval painless, converting what could have been a long approval chain into one walkthrough. On a 220-room rollout, that single afternoon was the highest-leverage step of the program.

Retrofit in an occupied building

The property stays open throughout the renovation, so installation happens floor by floor, outside event schedules. That constraint drove the engineering: retrofit-friendly mounting, consistent performance across hundreds of rooms, and centralized maintenance reporting so the facilities team sees the whole estate from one log. Renovation cycles, not just new builds, are what this line is engineered for.

What the stations pour

The drinking stations draw on the wall-mounted and built-in series: instant hot water where the property wants tea service, chilled water on demand, and purification stages matched to the venue's water quality. Engineering teams also care about the quiet numbers — service access, duty cycles between events, and what happens when a unit needs attention mid-occupancy. Those parameters were specified alongside the visible ones, which is what separates a renovation-friendly program from a hardware drop. Consistency is the specification that matters most at check-in: a guest on the third floor and a guest on the twenty-third should never notice the difference.

What moves into production now

With sampling approved, production covers the full 220-room scope: wall-mounted units for the rooms, built-in stations for corridors and back-of-house, finish-matched trims, and the spare-parts package that backs the one-year program warranty. Rollout is phased with the renovation calendar, targeting completion ahead of the events season. The order book reads 220 rooms; the engineering reads like a venue — corridors, back-of-house, event floors, all pouring to the same spec.

What the project taught us

  • Write the spec against the interior package — at hotel scale, finish decisions are engineering decisions.
  • Mock-up rooms convert approval chains into walkthroughs; on hundreds of rooms, that is the highest-leverage step available.
  • Occupied-building retrofit rewards floor-by-floor planning outside event schedules.
  • Centralized maintenance reporting is not an add-on for hotel groups — it is part of the product.

The first production batch is on schedule. We will report back when the rollout completes — ahead of the events season, if the current pace holds. If you are renovating a property, the structure travels: one spec written against your interiors, one mock-up room, phased floors, central reporting. Bring the calendar; the engineering adapts to it.
